children.html: The central role of self-reassurance to explain body and eating attitudes
Ana Laura Mendes1 · Cláudia Ferreira1 · Inês A. Trindade1
Received: 2 January 2018 / Accepted: 17 August 2018 © Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2018

Literature has emphasized the significant role of social acceptance and connectedness in well-being and the benefits of cultivating a positive body image in the prevention and treatment of body and eating-related difficulties. The current study aims to examine whether strategies of self-reassurance and body-image appreciation mediate the association of feelings of social safeness and acceptance with the "core" dimensions of body and eating-related psychopathology (restraint, eating concern, weight concern, and shape concern), while controlling the effects of body mass index (BMI). Participants were 309 Portuguese women, aged between 18 and 50 years that completed self-report measures. Results from the performed path analysis revealed that self-reassurance and body-image appreciation mediated the impact of feelings of social safeness and acceptance on eating psychopathology-related dimensions. Results seem to suggest that women who perceive the self as acceptable and desirable tend to adopt self-reassurance strategies. These strategies in turn seem to predict a protective and caring relationship with one's own body and decreased severity of eating psychopathology symptoms. This path model explained 22%, 27%, 51%, and 47% of restraint, eating concern, weight concern, and shape concern, respectively, and showed an excellent model fit. Our findings appear to offer significant insights in the field of body and eating-related psychopathology and seem to support the pertinence of creating intervention programs for women from the general community with body and eating-related difficulties that encourage the adoption of self-reassurance strategies and promote a positive and respectful relationship with one's own body image.
Level of evidence V, cross-sectional descriptive study.
Keywords Social safeness · Self-reassurance · Body appreciation · Body-image concerns · Disordered eating

According to an evolutionary perspective, the need to be valued, chosen, and accepted by others is a fundamental and universal aspect in human's motivation [1]. When individuals present qualities that are valued by their social group, they can experience important social advantages (such as favorable appreciation from others and a sense of belonging and connectedness [2]). In accordance with the social rank theory [3] and the sociometer theory [4], most of the

psychological difficulties or problems are rooted in perceptions of a lack of social acceptance. In fact, low social rank (e.g., feelings of inferiority, incompetency, unfavourable social comparisons, and the tendency to perceive the self as undesirable and subordinated) may play a crucial role in the development of several psychological conditions, namely, eating disorders [5–7].

Body image and weight overconcerns may arise from the perception of being in an unsafe position in relation to one's social group. Specifically, body and eating-related disordered attitudes and behaviours may be conceptualized as maladaptive defensive responses to overcome social threats (such as being ostracized or rejected due to one's body shape or weight [6, 8]) and to compete for others' acceptance and positive attention [8–10]. In fact, recent research has highlighted that the absence of feelings of warmth and safeness in current social relationships is associated with the need to

control or conceal unwanted body-image features, to assure acceptance by significant others [11].

Supportive contexts, in which individuals perceive their social world as kind, warm, and safe, seem to facilitate the adoption of adaptive emotion strategies, particularly to cope with stress and personal failures [12]. Furthermore, research has shown that social safeness is inversely related to negative emotional states (such as feelings of inferiority and shame) and maladaptive regulation processes (such as submission, and self-criticism [13, 14]). Experiences of safeness and social connectedness, which arise in response to the presence of acceptance, caring, and affiliation signals from others [14, 15], seem to protect individuals against disordered behaviours (such as threat-focused responses and competition strategies [16]). Particularly, the literature has emphasized the powerful effect of these positive emotions on emotional maturation, affects regulation and emotional well-being [12], and seems to promote the adoption of caring, kind, and soothing attitudes towards the self (e.g., selfreassurance [12, 17]).

Self-reassurance characterizes the ability to be warm, caring, and supportive to the self (by, for example focusing on one's positive features) when things go wrong and in the face of failures or setbacks [18]. This ability represents a positive emotion regulation process and seems to be an alternative response to deal with feelings of inferiority and personal failures by encouraging active coping strategies and promoting overall well-being and health [19].

Empirical data have shown that the ability to be kind and to accept perceived defects is positively associated with selfcompassion, positive affect, quality of life, and with better psychological health [12, 18, 20], and negatively linked with negative outcomes, such as body shame, body dissatisfaction, and disordered eating [21, 22].

Body appreciation is defined by a caring and protective relationship with one's own body. Indeed, this innovative construct is characterized by accepting attitudes and favorable opinions towards one's own body image, regardless of its appearance [21, 23]. This positive body-related attitude seems to protect one against unrealistic media standards related to physical appearance and the pressure present in Western Societies to be thin, and has been consistently linked with several indicators of well-being [21, 24]. In fact, a recent body of research has highlighted the benefits of the cultivation of positive body image for the prevention and treatment of eating disorders.

The present study intended to expand previous research [25] about the relationship between emotion regulation strategies, body appreciation, and disordered eating attitudes and behaviours. More specifically, the main aim of current study was to test an integrative model that explored whether the relationship between social safeness and body appreciation and the "core" dimensions of body and eating-related

psychopathology (restraint, eating concern, weight concern, and shape concern) is mediated through the mechanisms of self-reassurance while controlling the effect of BMI. We expected that higher levels of social safeness are associated with lower levels of the severity of eating psychopathology symptoms through higher levels of self-reassurance and body appreciation.

Participants were 309 Portuguese women from the general population, aged between 18 and 50 (M=23.00 years; SD 6.37) years and a mean of 13.54 (SD 1.56) years of education. Concerning body mass index (BMI), participants reported a mean of 22.28 (SD 3.09), which corresponds to a normal-weighted sample [26]. More specifically, 22 participants (7.12%) were underweight (BMI≤18.5), 239 (77.35%) presented normal weight (18.5≤BMI≥25.0) and 48 (15.53%) were overweight (BMI≥25.0), which corresponds to a normal-weighted sample on average [27].
The body mass index was calculated from participant's selfreported current weight and height using the Quetelet Index (kg/m2 ).

The SSPS was developed to assess the extent in which individuals experience feelings of social safeness (that is the perception of being accepted and valued by others, with a sense of safeness and warmth). Respondents rate their agreement with 11 statements (e.g., "I feel connected to others") using a 5-point Likert scale from 1 ("almost never") to 5 ("almost all the time"). This scale presented an internal consistency of α=0.92 in the original version [16]. In our study, we achieved an internal consistency of 0.96.
The Forms of Self-criticizing and Self-reassuring Scale (FSCRS [18, 29])

The FSCRS is a self-report instrument design to assess people's critical and reassuring evaluative responses to failures, setbacks or when things go wrong. It comprises 22 items and measures two forms of self-criticism: inadequate self and hated self and one form of self-soothe: self-reassurance subscale (e.g., "I can still feel lovable and acceptable.").

Participants were asked to select, in a five-point Likert scale (0="Not at all like me" to 4="Extremely like me"), the extent to which each statement applies to their experience. In the original study, Cronbach' alpha values were 0.90 for the inadequate-self subscale and 0.86 for hated self and reassured self, respectively [18]. Similarly, alpha coefficients for the Portuguese version were 0.89 for the inadequate-self subscale, 0.87 for reassured self, and 0.72 for hated self [29]. In the current study, we only used the self-reassurance subscale, which presented a Cronbach alpha of 0.91.

BAS-2 is a ten-item self-report measure that assess acceptance and loving attitudes towards one's body's features, even if not totally pleased with all its aspects (e.g., "I feel that my body has at least some good qualities"). This scale revealed an excellent internal consistency, reported Cronbach's alpha values of 0.97 and 0.95 for the original and the Portuguese versions, respectively. In the present study, the Cronbach's alpha was 0.94.

The EDE-Q is a 36-item self-report measure that evaluates the frequency and intensity of eating pathology-related attitudes and behaviours. It comprises four subscales: (1) restraint; (2) eating concern; (3) shape concern; and (4) weight concern. The items are rated for the frequency of occurrence or for the severity. The global EDE-Q score can also be obtained by calculating the mean of the four subscales. This measure presented good psychometric properties in both the original and the Portuguese versions (α=0.94). In the present study, the global and subscale's score of EDE-Q presented a Cronbach's alpha ranging from 0.77 to 0.95.

The current study was part of a wider Portuguese project about the role of different emotion regulation processes on mental health and eating attitudes and behaviours. All ethical and deontological requirements inherent to scientific research were respected. The study aims, procedures, and confidentiality of the data were fully explained to the potential participants, and those wanting to take part in the study provided their written informed consent, before the completion of the self-report instruments (approximately 15 min).

Participants were recruited through online advertisements, via a social network (Facebook) and by e-mail invitations. Self-report questionnaires were initially completed by 509 individuals of both genders (352 women and 157 men), with ages ranging from 18 to 60 years. According

to the purpose of this study, only 309 Portuguese women, with ages ranging from 18 to 50 years, were selected. The data cleaning procedure excluded: (a) male participants and (b) participants who were younger than 18 or older than 50 years.

The Software IBM SPSS (v.22: SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL) was used to perform descriptive and correlational analyses, and path analysis was conducted using the software AMOS (Analysis of Momentary Structure, v.22; SPSS Inc., Chicago IL).

Descriptive statistics (means and standard deviations) were conducted to examine the characteristics of the final sample in the study variables. In addition, product–moment Pearson correlation analyses were performed to explore the associations between feelings of social safeness (SSPS), self-reassurance (FSCRS_reassure), body appreciation (BAS-2), and eating psychopathology (EDE-Q). The magnitudes of these correlations were analyzed considering Cohen's guidelines, in which magnitudes between 0.1 and 0.3 were considered weak, between 0.3 and 0.5 were moderate, and magnitudes above 0.5 were strong, considering a significance level of 0.05 [32].

Finally, path analyses were conducted to test whether the association between social safeness (exogenous variable) and disordered eating attitudes and behaviours (measured through four subscales of EDE-Q; endogenous variable) would be mediated by self-reassurance and body appreciation (endogenous mediator variables) while controlling for BMI. To test the estimation of the significance of the regression coefficients and fit statistics, the Maximum Likelihood estimation method was selected. Moreover, several goodness-of-fit indices were computed to examine the credibility of the model: Chi square (χ2 /df; that suggests a good fit with 2–5), the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), and the Tucker–Lewis Index (TLI), with values above 0.90 indicating good fit and the root-mean square error of approximation (RMSEA; which indicates a good adjustment when values range between 0.05 and 0.08 [33, 34]). The Bootstrap resampling method, with 5000 Bootstrap samples, and 95% confidence interval (CI) around the standardized estimates of direct, indirect, and total effects, was performed to test the significance of the mediational paths. The effects were considered as significantly different from zero (p < 0.050) if zero was not included in the interval between the lower and the upper bound of the 95% bias-corrected confidence interval [35]. Effects with p<0.050 were considered statistically significant.

Univariate and multivariate normalities were examined by the values of skewness (Sk) and Kurtosis (Ku). The skewness values ranged from −0.14 to 0.96 (in the FSCRS_reassure and BMI, respectively), while the values of Kurtosis ranged from −0.22 to 1.56 (in EDE-Q and BMI, respectively). According to Kline [35], these results revealed that there was no severe violation of the normal distribution of the data (z-scores: SK<|3| and Ku<|8–10|).

The means and standard deviations of the study variables are reported in Table 1. Product–moment Pearson correlation coefficients indicated that BMI revealed to be negatively associated with body appreciation and positively correlated with eating psychopathology, with weak and moderate magnitudes, respectively. However, a non-significant relationship was found between BMI and social safeness and self-reassurance. Furthermore, positive correlations were found between social safeness and self-reassurance and body appreciation, with strong and moderate magnitudes, respectively. In addition, self-reassurance was significantly and positively associated, with a strong correlation, with body appreciation.
In turn, social safeness, self-reassurance, and body appreciation presented a negative association with EDE-Q, with weak, moderate, and strong correlations, respectively.
Finally, concerning the EDE-Q's subscales (restraint, eating concern, shape concern, and weight concern), positive associations, from weak to moderate magnitudes, were

found with BMI. With SSPS, self-reassurance and, BAS-2, the EDE-Q's subscales correlated negatively, with weak to high correlations. In addition, positive associations were found between EDE-Q's subscales and the global score of EDE-Q.

Path analysis was performed to explore whether the mechanisms of self-reassurance and body appreciation act as significant mediators of the associations established between social safeness and the "core" dimensions of body and eating-related psychopathology (restraint, eating concern, weight concern, and shape concern) while controlling for the effect of body mass index (BMI).

The path model was tested through a fully saturated initial model (i.e., with zero degrees of freedom), consisting of 44 parameters. However, seven paths were not significant: the direct effect of social safeness on eating concern (bsocial safeness=0.00; SEb=0.01; Z=0.00, p=0.998), the direct effect of body mass index on self-reassurance (bBMI=−0.06; SEb=0.01; Z=−0.66, p=0.512), the direct effect of self-reassurance on restraint (bself−reassurance=0.02; SEb = 0.01; Z = 1.08, p = 0.280), on weight concern (bself−reassurance=0.02; SEb=0.01; Z=1.52, p=0.128), on eating concern (bself−reassurance=0.01; SEb=0.01; Z=0.92, p = 0.358), and on shape concern (bself−reassurance= 0.01; SEb=0.01; Z=0.84, p=0.399), and the direct effect of social safeness on restraint (bsocial safeness=0.01; SEb=0.01; Z=1.41, p=0.159). These paths were eliminated, and the model readjusted.

Specifically, to what concerns direct effects, results showed that social safeness had direct effects of 0.57 (b=0.36; SE_b=0.03; Z=12.18; p<0.001), 0.12 (b=0.09; SE_b = 0.04; Z = 2.55; p < 0.050), -0.16 (b = -0.02; SE_b = 0.01; Z = -4.79; p < 0.001), and -0.15 (b = -0.02; SE_b = 0.01; Z = -4.28; p < 0.001) on self-reassurance, body appreciation, weight concern, and shape concern, respectively. In turn, self-reassurance presented a direct effect of 0.65 (b = 0.79; SE_b = 0.06; Z = 13.98; p < 0.001) on body appreciation. Finally, body appreciation had direct effects of -0.36 (b = -0.05; SE_b = 0.01; Z = -6.96; p < 0.001), -0.47 (b = -0.06; SE_b = 0.01; Z = -9.44; p < 0.001), -0.60 (b = -0.12; SE_b = 0.01; Z = -13.65; p < 0.001) and -0.63(b = -0.13; SE_b = 0.01; Z = -13.81; p < 0.001) on restraint, eating concern, weight concern, and shape concern, respectively.

The analysis revealed that social safeness had an indirect effect on body appreciation of 0.37 (95% CI 0.30–0.44, p < 0.001), which was partially mediated by self-reassurance. In turn, social safeness presented indirect effects of -0.17 (95% CI -0.23 to -0.12, p < 0.001) and of -0.23

(95% CI -0.28 to -0.17, p < 0.001) on restraint and eating concern, respectively, which were totally mediated by self-reassurance and body appreciation. Social safeness also presented indirect effects of -0.29 (95% CI -0.36 to -0.23, p < 0.001) and of -0.31 (95% CI -0.38 to -0.24, p < 0.001) on weight concern and shape concern, respectively, which were partially mediated by self-reassurance and body appreciation. Finally, indirect effects of -0.23 (95% CI -0.31 to -0.16, p < 0.001), -0.30 (95% CI -0.37 to -0.23, p < 0.001), -0.39 (95% CI -0.47 to -0.31, p < 0.001), and -0.41 (95% CI -0.49 to -0.33, p < 0.001) were found between self-reassurance and restraint, eating concern, weight concern, and shape concern, respectively, which were totally mediated by body appreciation.
To sum up, the final model demonstrated that the impact of social safeness on the severity of eating psychopathology symptoms was partially carried through self-reassurance and body appreciation.

The support and care of others are theorized as having a major impact on one's genetic expression and one's sense of self [15]. Not feeling accepted and cared for may be perceived as a threat and has been associated with poor psychological adjustment and with several psychosocial problems

[13, 16]. Furthermore, when individuals perceive their social world as unsafe and threatening, they tend to adopt defensive responses, such as trying to conceal, or control characteristics thought to be perceived by others as unwanted or undesirable [36, 37]. Body-image features are often the target of such evaluations, and the engagement in eating psychopathology often emerges to "correct" those features and to assure positive attention from others [38]. Extensive literature has focused on the predictors of disordered eating, but the study of its protective factors has yet been scarcely studied.

The present study, conducted in a sample of 309 Portuguese women, thus aimed to test an innovative model that explored the effects of known positive psychological variables on the severity of eating psychopathology symptoms. More specifically, the current study intended to examine the relationship between social safeness and connectedness, self-reassurance strategies, body-image appreciation, and the engagement in eating restraint or attempts to restraint one's eating, concerns about eating, shape, and weight. In this way, a path model was conducted to analyses whether the link between social safeness and disordered eating attitudes and behaviours is carried by the mechanisms of self-reassurance and body appreciation while controlling for participants' BMI.

Results showed that feelings of social safeness are linked with the ability of being self-reassuring to the self, that is, the capacity of being caring and supportive to oneself. It thus seems that the perception of one's social world as safe and caring may be associated with the development of adaptive emotion regulation strategies, such as self-reassurance, which goes in line with the previous literature [12]. Our findings go further in line with prior research by demonstrating that social safeness is associated with the experience of a positive, caring, and protective relationship towards one's body. These findings further corroborated prior studies that emphasizes the positive association between social safeness and the experience of close emotional bonds with family, peers, and romantic partners positive body image [11, 25, 39]. Moreover, the main contribution of study is the demonstration that the association between social safeness and body appreciation is mediated by the mechanisms of self-reassurance. Indeed, it seems that the impact of social safeness on the perception of one's body image is partially explained by the ability to adopt of a caring, warm, and safe relationship with the self when things go wrong.

In addition, our results further explored the role of these emotion regulation processes on the overimportance of body weight, shape and eating, and the engagement in disordered eating (e.g., restraint or attempts to restraint one's eating). Our findings seem to indicate that even though social safeness and connectedness have a significant direct impact on body-image-related dimensions of EDE-Q, it

main potential positive effect on the severity of eating psychopathology symptoms is carried by the protective effects of self-reassurance and caring and protective relationship with one's own body. Indeed, it was revealed that the known association between social safeness and body appreciation and lower levels of the severity of eating psychopathology symptoms [25] is mediated by the adaptive mechanisms of self-reassurance, in a model that explained 22, 27, 51, and 47% of restraint, eating concern, weight concern, and shape concern, respectively. These findings may indicate that the protective effect of social safeness on eating psychology is mostly explained by these adaptive emotion regulation processes (i.e., self-reassurance and body appreciation). In other words, the perceiving the world as safe and secure may have a protective effect on the engagement in disordered eating, through the development of adaptive strategies to deal with failures or difficulties, such as self-reassurance and a positive relationship with one's physical appearance. In this way, interventions aiming to prevent or treat eating psychopathology may benefit from promoting these emotion regulation processes, especially in women.

This study contained some limitations that set the stage for future research. First, the main limitation is the use of a cross-sectional design that limits the establishment of causal directions between the study's variables [40]. Future studies are needed to analyses the nature and directionally of the associations between variables over time. Another limitation is the exclusive use of self-report measures, which may be susceptible to biases. It would be important to include other non-self-report measures (e.g., structured interviews) to corroborate our findings. In addition, the selection of a sample exclusively composed of women from the Portuguese general population prevents the generalization of the results. Thus, although the engagement in disordered eating-related attitudes and behaviours is more prevalent among women, future studies should replicate our hypotheses in different samples, namely, male (through other measures validates for males) and clinical samples (e.g., eating disorder patients). Furthermore, multi-group analyses that explore the variance or invariance of the tested model in distinct categories of body mass index (underweight, normal, overweight, and obese) should be explored in upcoming studies.

The results from the present study are nonetheless of interest as they offer new insights on the protective mechanisms of social safeness, self-reassurance, and positive body image against body shape and weight concerns and their control through the overevaluation of eating and the engagement in restraint strategies. In this study, self-reassurance emerges as a relevant regulation process that future research should analyses as a possible predictor of meaningful change in body-image attitudes and eating psychopathology levels. To sum up, by focusing on the study of protective mechanisms in relation to body and eating difficulties, these results

seem to provide important guidelines for the development of preventive and therapeutic intervention programs. Furthermore, this research emphasizes the importance of promoting self-reassurance and self-compassion skills, which seem to be crucial to the development of attitudes of acceptance and respect regarding body-image features, and for the adoption of heathy eating behaviours.
